opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's something we thought about quite a lot. With the earlier Genie work, the original Genie paper and then Genie 2, the models were genuinely capable of generating interactive environments: you could take an action and the world would respond in a consistent way. But they weren't running in real time. There was latency between your input and the next frame, and the interactions were relatively short.

So when we announced that work, we tried to be really careful to frame it as research. We weren't saying "here's a game engine you can play." We were saying "here's evidence that a learned world model can be action-controllable, that it can generalize from a single image prompt, that it can maintain some consistency." Those were the scientific claims, and we wanted the communication to match them.

Part of that was just being explicit in the blog posts and papers about what was and wasn't happening. The videos people saw were generated interactively, but not at a frame rate you'd consider playable. We tried to say that clearly rather than let people assume.

I think there's always a tension, though. When you show video of something that looks like a game, people's mental model is immediately "I can play this." And that's understandable. So you have to be proactive about setting expectations, because otherwise the gap between what people imagine and what the system actually does becomes a source of disappointment, or worse, people feel misled.

What's been nice is that the progression has validated that framing. We could say, look, this is a step on a path, and real-time interaction is one of the things we're working toward. Then when we got to a point where the model could actually run in real time, that became a meaningful milestone in its own right rather than something people thought we'd already had. So being honest early actually made the later progress more legible.

More broadly, I think in this field we have a responsibility not to overclaim. World models are exciting, and it's easy for the hype to run ahead of the reality. If we want people, researchers especially, to trust our results, being clear about the limitations is part of that.

r001.rationale: The response says leading with research framing and being honest about limitations helped set expectations, but it does not say that foregrounding the lack of real-time playability could reduce the announcement’s excitement.

r002.rationale: The response says game-like videos can make viewers assume the system is playable. It does not say that viewers may miss a disclosure because it appears later in the announcement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we thought about quite a lot, actually. With the original Genie, and even with Genie 2, we were really trying to be upfront that these were research prototypes. The first Genie was trained on internet video of 2D platformers, and it ran at something like one frame per second. It wasn't something you could sit down and play. So in the blog post and the paper we were quite explicit that this was a proof of concept, that the point was to show you could learn an action space purely from unlabeled video, not that we had a product.

But I think the honest answer is that it's hard, because people see a video clip and their brain fills in the rest. You show a sequence of frames where a character jumps in response to an action, and it looks like a game. And so the natural reaction is, "Can I play it?" And the answer at the time was, well, not really, not in any way that would feel satisfying. We had to kind of keep saying that.

With Genie 2 we moved to 3D and much longer horizons, and the quality jumped a lot, but it was still not real time. We were generating these clips offline, and we tried to be clear about that in the release. We deliberately showed things like the model being prompted and then an agent or a human providing actions, but we framed it as "here's what the model can do" rather than "here's something you can go use." I think there's a responsibility there, especially coming from a lab like DeepMind, not to overpromise.

And honestly, part of the reason we felt comfortable being so open about the limitations is that we saw them as temporary. The research trajectory was pretty clear to us internally. Each version was a step toward interactivity, and so with Genie 3, when we actually got to real time at twenty-four frames per second, that was the moment where the framing could change. We could finally say, this is something you can actually interact with. So in a way, being upfront early made that later announcement land more meaningfully, because people could see the progression rather than feeling like they'd been sold something that wasn't there yet.

r001.rationale: The candidate says audiences naturally ask whether the prototypes are playable and emphasizes being upfront about limitations, but does not say that leading with the lack of real-time playability would undermine excitement.

r002.rationale: It notes that people see a video clip and imagine a game, but does not say that compelling videos can cause audiences to miss a disclosure placed later in the announcement.

astra-6.text: I think you have to be very clear about what the system can actually do. With the earlier Genie research, you could choose actions and generate what happened next, but that didn’t mean you could sit down and play it in real time. And if you show a video without explaining that distinction, it’s very easy for people to assume that’s the experience they’d get. So I’d make that limitation explicit alongside the demo. The exciting result was learning an action-controllable world from video; real-time playability was still a separate challenge.

sol-6.1.text: I think you have to be really clear about what the system can and can’t do. With the earlier Genie work, you could choose an action and the model would generate what happened next, but that didn’t mean it was running at a speed where you could sit down and play it like a video game. If you show a video playing smoothly, people can understandably assume that’s the experience they’d have. So it’s important to distinguish the generated video from the time it took to generate it, and to communicate that alongside the demo. The exciting research result was the ability to learn an action-controllable world from video; real-time playability was a separate challenge.
